articles.title: Dr. Jill Lepore on why AI backlash is vital for the future
articles.description: Today, I’m talking with Harvard professor and New Yorker staff writer Dr. Jill Lepore about her new book, The Rise and Fall of the Artificial State, which comes out on August 25. Jill is one of the best writers there is at identifying institutional patterns in history, and Decoder is a show about systems, so this book could not possibly be more in our zone. You build systems by measuring things — gathering information, quantifying it as data, and taking action on it. And Jill’s big thesis in the book is that this kind of systemic measurement is really a dehumanizing act, one that flattens human concerns into something, well, artificial. These artificial structures touch everything — not just in the more obvious places like in apps or AI, but all the way up to politics and governance itself, and Jill’s insights here are a telling portrait of the way Big Tech and its billionaire figureheads have managed to break the very idea of the state itself. Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here. You’ll hear Jill tell me she wanted to write a “kind of grumpy book,” but in my reading, it’s a pretty dead-ahead look at the last century and a half of technological and social developments and how we got to a place where bots are maybe running everything. Jill’s idea of the artificial state starts with the very idea of quantification, from the first stabs at taking a census thousands of years ago to the invention of modern political polling in the 1930s. But where she really sees a big pivot — and the era she and I talked about most — is in the 1980s, when we saw the emergence of the Silicon Valley culture we have today, when computers got personal, and when computer-aided targeting and microtargeting really truly became both possible and commonplace, both for ads and for political campaigns. What Jill and I did disagree about is some of her pessimism about the internet, because the internet is what made jobs and careers like mine — and businesses like The Verge, and shows like Decoder — even possible at all. There really was a great democratizing of access that happened in the late 20th century and into the 21st, as people got online, and not all of it was as illusory as maybe the great hopes for Twitter after the Arab Spring turned out to be. But as I said, Jill thinks in systems, and so her response, about the way systems of power keep adapting to how people use new technology, was as illuminating as ever. Of course, we also talked about the future — including where she thinks she still sees hope for the future. And yes, that does include college kids booing the AI CEOs at graduation ceremonies. Okay: Dr Jill Lepore, on the Artificial State. Here we go. This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity. Dr. Jill Lepore, you’re a staff writer at The New Yorker, you’re a professor of history and law at Harvard University, and most importantly, you’re the author of a new book, The Rise and Fall of the Artificial State. Welcome to Decoder. Hey, thanks for having me. I am really excited to talk to you. I’m a big fan of your work over the years. And I have to say, this book is one of the most Decoder-y, Verge-y, Nilay-Patel-strike-zone books of all time. [Laughs] Wow. I’m not sure how to take that, but I guess that’s good. The producers and I just had a thrill ride reading this book. It is essentially about how computers and measurement flatten us and then systems can take advantage of that flattening. Like I said, it’s in the strike zone. So let’s just start at the very beginning for folks. The book is called The Rise and Fall of the Artificial State. Tell us what the “artificial state” is. Define it so we can start from that foundation. What I mean by the artificial state is a successor to the liberal nation-state, the constitutional democracy under which our freedom of speech, free discourse, and constitutional rights are central to our experience as citizens within a nation-state. We talk a lot about democratic decay and democratic backsliding, and there’s a whole public discussion of what’s happening with democracy, but I don’t think we talk about the nation-state as much as we might. And that is to say the state itself. And so what I mean by the ‘artificial state’ is a state in which more and more of the functions of the nation-state have been taken over by private multinational corporations. The easiest example of that to think about is what is euphemistically called the public square, which is where people get information about how to vote, what’s going on in the world, how to make decisions, and how to exercise their rights and duties as citizens. Our public discourse is almost entirely privatized and owned by corporations. As many, many people have demonstrated — it’s not news to your listeners or to anyone — the priority of public discourse is not the free expression of ideas and democratic deliberation, it is the monetization of attention and of outrage. More than that, a fairly recent vintage is the fact that public platforms in which we exchange ideas as citizens and democracies are dominated by bots. All of them have been inverted for several years now, or different numbers of years, from X to Facebook to TikTok. There are far more bots than humans on those platforms. Many of those bots are owned by corporations and have particular acts, their own kind of financial interests, but they’re owned by state actors, non-state actors, criminals, and terrorists. What we’re at risk of is losing the liberal constitutional democracy and having it become supplanted by what I describe as the artificial state. One of the things that really struck me about this is at least America’s conception of itself, the United States’ conception of itself is this messy, multi-part democracy. The Senate loves to call itself the most deliberative body in the history of the world, and it’s supposed to be a whole bunch of people that are ruled by the consent of the governed and we’re all arguing. Your thesis is that that’s what we say about ourselves, but actually we’ve automated away and numerically quantified away a bunch of that, and we are now run maybe by bots on Twitter, or at least politicians are overwhelmed by bots on Twitter and they’ve outsourced their thinking, or there are consultants that are turning us all into polling data. Is that the trajectory we’re on that ends the nation-state? Is that the core of the idea? Yeah. It has a long history, but the acceleration of these developments in the age of artificial intelligence is really considerable. I’ll give you two examples that stretch out across a century. In the 1930s, we see the invention of so-called scientific polling. George Gallup starts the American Institute of Public Opinion research in 1935. What polling does gradually over the middle decades of the 20th century is replace the kind of door-to-door precinct walking that campaigns would need to do, right? If I’m running for election in some neighborhood, I have to go talk to people. I’m going to go to baseball games, basketball games, and the public library. But increasingly, it became less necessary for political campaigns to do that because they could subcontract out political polling. You can find out what political opinion is in a neighborhood if you want to run a campaign just by doing data mining and data analysis. We might say, “That makes politics so much more efficient. Those campaigns can more efficiently use their money and they can get their message out to the right people.” But if you think about each one of those conversations that people used to have — “I’m a campaign volunteer and I’m going to go and I’m going to sit in on some PTA meeting,” or, “I’m going to go to a basketball game in some neighborhood and talk to the parents who are there” — all those conversations are the civic glue that holds a civil society together. Replacing that chatting under a street lamp about, “What do you think about this guy?” with just extracting data, which is where we are now, is a much more artificial politics than we have had before. There’s been great coverage lately of emerging trends for the 2026 election in the US,and around the world, where a lot of people report that even in these primaries that have been going on over the spring and summer, they’ll ask ChatGPT, “How should I vote in the primary?” Meanwhile, many of the campaign messages that you’re getting have been crafted by artificial intelligence. The fact that you are getting them is a decision made by artificial intelligence. In a way, it’s AI versus AI in these upcoming elections, or even in elections that are already transpiring. You can see how you could fall into that step, just going downhill on skis. But I wanted to write a grumpy book to say, “Let’s pause for a minute. What’s at the bottom of that hill? Is that an icy pond and we’re going to just go through the ice and we’re all going to drown in there? Or is that a beautiful new political world?” And I think it looks pretty perilous. The book traces this evolution step by step as you’re describing; this is a slow build to maybe where we’ve gotten today. As you point out several times in the book, there are a bunch of science fiction authors in the ’50s and ’60s who were looking at computers and drawing a picture of the future. Some of them picked utopia, and there are entire movements about technocratic utopia that emerge, and a lot of them pick dystopia. They draw a picture of computer-aided dystopia. You point this out. Everyone has heard the Torment Nexus meme. It’s in the book. You use it in the book. Our modern industrialists have read dystopian science fiction and decided that is the model of the future that they’re attempting to build. I’m curious why you think they’ve all gotten it wrong, from Elon Musk to Peter Thiel on down, and if that is an inflection point for us to actually pick a different future. It’s a big thing, starting in the ’30s, to imagine a future in which the president of the United States is chosen by a machine. There are a bunch of examples of this from the ’30s, where people are really worried about totalitarianism and the dehumanization of people as a consequence of the machine age. But there’s also a lot of this in the 1950s. For instance, a classic story by Isaac Asimov that I think is from 1955, called “Franchise,” and it’s set on the days before November 4th, 2008, the day Obama won the presidency. In that imagined future, there’s this machine called the Multivac that determines, using polling data, who in the United States is the average man, the most representative man. The sampling method that pollsters use has been perfected mathematically by this computer to pick the average person. And that’s the only person who votes. And then that guy has to go into hiding because if people don’t like who was elected or the presidency goes badly, his life is destroyed. There’s a lot of this stuff in science fiction, but Sam Altman was on Joe Rogan and he started talking about how great it would be if AI chose the president of the United States. Yes, he was fucking around, but he was also serious. “Wouldn’t that be great? Because it’s so efficient and we don’t have to bother and it spares us the labor.” And that general premise, that “Why would we bother to do something that a machine can do for us?” without the realization that the rest of us would have. There are some things we want to do, including meaningful work: writing, making art, and doing things for ourselves. I know these are very smart people, but they’re not humanists. Thiel would say that he’s a political philosopher. I’m not so convinced of that. The capacity for humanistic inquiry, reading, and reasoning is not something you see in great evidence in that culture. It’s been bred out, in a way, of the culture of Silicon Valley. Even if you look back to the ’90s and the culture of the celebration of the serial entrepreneur as the new man of progress, that particular kind of cultural formulation was all about the disavowal of the past. It doesn’t matter what came before. You want to start a ride service, you don’t study taxis or figure out where delivery service came from. You don’t look at traffic patterns. You don’t study anything in the past, you just start new. You just imagine it all new and you destroy what came before. There’s such a rejection of the knowledge and wisdom of earlier human beings. The posture of the humanist is one of humility. Isn’t it magisterial and majestic how Homer wrote The Odyssey so long ago and it’s still so powerful? The timelessness of literature and the arts, the infinite beauty of humanity’s capacity for making things, it’s just not the ethos. It’s, “No, we’ll do it better. It doesn’t matter what anybody did before.” It’s, “We’re innovating, we’re disrupting.” The culture so fetishizes the future that it doesn’t have that, “Let’s listen to what other people who came before might have known, that’s still wisdom.” That makes for a very poor reading of literature. We could have a great argument about what Isaac Asimov meant by that story. It’s not a determinant, I’m not the authority on Isaac Asimov, but I’m not going to ask Sam Altman what a short story means. Well, he would just ask ChatGPT. That’s right. There’s something very interesting about this cast of characters, particularly Peter Thiel who comes up in your book, Elon Musk who comes up in your book somewhere over 100 times I think. They are falling back to literally Catholicism as some kind of moral foundation for whatever decisions they’re making. And whether or not they’re misreading Catholicism is irrelevant to them. They’re often in fights with the Pope, which is just not something a straight reading of Catholicism would allow you to do. There’s an entire culture of thinking — I won’t call it a philosophy, because I don’t think it’s quite that developed — around first principles. “We’re going to do first principles thinking and that will lead us to some disruptive outcome.” It often, to me at least, feels like where that first principle begins is a choice about what to ignore from the past. I see that over again in your book, in the culture we live in at large, that deciding what to set aside is the big decision. That’s an assumption that is often not questioned as we go step by step towards a more quantified society, a more automated society. But there’s something messy about democracy that is very, very important. The decision we’re making now is to actually set that mess aside in the name of, I don’t know, efficiency, potentially happiness. I’m curious if you see that setting-aside is happening by accident or on purpose? I think of these guys as really instrumental. They’re not pursuing knowledge for its own sake. They are deeply interested in exploration and wonder, and one of the things I really love about this moment is the fascination with space and space exploration, which I think is tremendously exciting. Harnessed to militarization in certain commercial projects is like, “Wow, we went from Star Trek to Star Wars really fast.” But the sense that what you might want to know about the world can be just because it’s worth knowing rather than that you can use it to extract money from other people, I just don’t think that’s part of that tech culture. It’s just not. A humanist commitment to knowledge for the sake of the accumulation of wisdom, leading a better life, and understanding the world with greater clarity and greater compassion is largely mocked in that world as “woke” or “feminine” or “libtard,” whatever. Especially with the conservative turn of the tech world, it takes on weird valances. It is really purposeful. “This kind of knowledge is not worth having [because] we can’t make money off of it. If we had that kind of knowledge, it might slow down what we’re trying to do. And what we’re trying to do is win the AI race and determine the future of humanity.” The lack of curiosity about the bigger world and the place of these really thrilling inventions within it, I don’t know, I find it bizarre. This causes a lot of self-reflection on my part. A lot of these people are my former students. I teach at Harvard. We send so many students off to work in Silicon Valley, and then they talk this way and what happened? What did we do wrong? Do you not have a sense of obligation to the human condition? You have a number of these markers. Walk us through some of them, from “the internet and social platforms will cause an outbreak of democracy” to where we are now in 2026. That first began to emerge in the 1980s. If you go back to 1984 and the launch of the Apple Macintosh and that famous, iconic Apple TV ad from the Super Bowl in January of 1984, the promise was that the personal computer would be revolutionary. As I’m sure you’ve talked about in your show and your audience really understands, the celebration of the personal computer as emancipation came out of the counterculture. There’s this great book, From Counterculture to Cyberculture, that’s about the so-called “California ideology” that marries counterculture libertarianism to computer utopianism. And you see that realized in 1984 with the launch of the Macintosh: “We’re going to defeat totalitarianism in the form of the giant mainframe IBM” that’s associated with two things at the time — big businesses, which are the only places that can afford these giant IBM mainframes that are running payroll systems and stuff for big corporations, and the Republican Party, which actually has a ton of IBM mainframes. The Democrats have basically no computers. It’s a huge problem for the Democrats in the 1970s and 1980s. So there’s this whole feeling that the personal computer is going to advance liberty, personal freedom, and therefore democracy. It’s a libertarian vision, but it’s about emancipation. And it’s an ad. At the end of the day, it’s just an ad campaign. There were people who said, “Well, exactly how does the personal computer emancipate? It’s great. I would like one. It’s fun to have. I also like a nice toaster, but my toaster isn’t going to emancipate me. What is it about?” You begin to see new tech computing products as very carefully packaged with an ideal about personal liberation. By the time you get to the ’90s, and the opening of the internet to commercial traffic, you see the scaling of that promise. “Now we all are going to have personal communities that are going to be linked to one another, and so society is going to become emancipated and democratized. We’re going to have a digital democracy.” Even though it’s a little bit like when political pundits make election forecasts and they’re wrong half the time, but no one ever remembers even what they forecasted. How do you even have a job? The people in the ’80s said the personal computer was going to liberate people. Well, it didn’t. But then in the ’90s, the internet was going to democratize societies. Well, it didn’t. That was just an ad campaign. And not that there aren’t plenty of people that sincerely believe that; there certainly is tremendous democratizing potential for the internet. There was a lot of promise there, but it’s not realized for all kinds of reasons. That’s already two strikes, but then you get to 2004 and all the emerging social media says, “Oh, Facebook, we’re going to democratize this. We’re going to connect everybody. Everyone will be able to be close to one another.” That also doesn’t happen. Then the ad campaign now, the packaging of somehow AI is going to do this. “What we need is democratic AI.” And that doesn’t mean we as a polity have a say, it just means that democratic countries should lift all restrictions and regulations so that democracies can have AI before authoritarians. It’s an old story. Can I push back on this a little bit? Because I personally struggle with that ad campaign, but the reality of it. There’s not a world previous to the internet where a guy like me who grew up in Wisconsin with no connections to the media ends up interviewing you, a Harvard professor. The internet needed to arrive. Publishing needed to be democratized. For whatever reason, AOL needed to pay a bunch of bloggers $12 a blog post, and then somehow decide that I should be one of those people. A lot of things had to happen where gatekeepers did fall away, and people like me were allowed to go find their audience. And I see it every single day now with young people who style themselves as creators or YouTubers, that they know that they can start a business and reach people on these platforms in some way. The flip side of that is that I do think a bunch of gatekeepers, the men who own these platforms — it’s largely men — realized they could turn the knobs. Elon Musk could buy X and he could take X from a platform where, when it was known as Twitter, lots and lots of activists could find each other and shape public opinion. And now X is whatever X is, and mostly racists find me. That’s my experience of that platform whenever I participate. Mark Zuckerberg started a Supreme Court for Facebook moderation because he wanted to recapitulate the machinations of democracy for people who had been banned for being crazy in their local Facebook groups. Maybe that worked and maybe it didn’t. My friend Casey Newton’s going to have something to write about in Platformer for the rest of his life as that experiment continues. But Zuckerberg said, “This is kind of dumb. I’m turning it off. We’re doing community notes here. No more moderation.” There’s some kind of pendulum swing. I agree with you, this is largely an ad campaign, but a lot of people were able to find each other. A lot of new people were allowed to gain a much larger platform with which to affect the culture, if not society at large. How do you put that in the context of the artificial state? I’ll just preview it. My next question is going to be about targeted advertising, which I think is an enormously influential piece of the puzzle. But it’s that dynamic that I struggle with, it’s not purely an ad campaign. I’ll come at that in a couple of different ways while granting that you absolutely have a point. I’ll figure out where we could maybe see a line. We tend to forget that, for instance, up until fairly recent history, maybe the 1980s, very few newspaper reporters in the United States had college degrees. They were people, mostly men, but there were a lot of women beat reporters and women editorial writers who started out delivering newspapers, working at the press, working the printer presses at newspapers, climbing their way up. I mean, there’s a reason Jimmy Olson is in the newsroom with Clark Kent in the 1930s comic books. They’re street kids and they know the streets and they start reporting. I don’t think they’re that different from coming up with a $12 blog post payment. That’s what happens in every industry, unsurprisingly. A new medium emerges, the daily paper or the twice-daily paper. The interview is invented. Eyewitness reporting is invented, the byline is invented. The history of the newspaper is all about an explosion of new kinds of doors that different people can walk through to report on the world to other people, and then more people can learn about the world because these newspapers are different. There’s an explosion in the democratization of any new technology of communication when it starts. By definition, if you can make a technology of communication cheaper and faster, you’re going to reach more people and more people are going to be involved in producing it. That happens with the first weekly newspapers, with the penny press in the 1830s, with the telegraph in the 1840s. It happens with how the telephone changes news reporting, the wire service in the Mexican-American War. It happens with the radio in the 1920s. It happens with TV in the 1950s. In fact, what’s interesting about that is that each of those transformations reshapes the party system. There have been seven party systems in American history and they all turn on a new emerging communications technology, which unsettles the relationship between the elites and the people. The people get more power. The parties just have to get realigned. But what always happens is the elites regain power. They don’t like it. They don’t like the news boys becoming beat reporters, becoming editors. They say, “Who are these nouveau people?” To use your metaphor, they turn the dial, they regain control, they consolidate their power over the medium, and then it has to wait for the next communications technology revolution. The tricky thing about the moment that we’re in now is the emerging technologies are not restoring power to the people. They’re not turning the wheel this way, they just keep going that way. I teach undergraduates. I see them go out in the world. There are no fucking jobs for them! You want to be a writer, you want to be an artist, you want to be a movie maker, you want to be a screenwriter, where are you going to get a job? The whole culture industry is imploding. I don’t think this is a magnificent time to be out there being an influencer. You still don’t have health insurance. You still can’t buy a house. I just don’t think we’re in a moment of emancipation that’s responding to that consolidation. Some people are like, “It’s great. I like that these billionaires have all this power over our culture.” I don’t, but we’re continuing to rotate in their direction. I don’t think it’s turning back. That’s how I would grant for you that there’s always something thrilling, emancipatory, illuminating, increasingly inclusive about a new communications technology. I wouldn’t deny that, and so you’re right to that degree, it’s not just an ad campaign, but I do think we’re in an exceptional moment right now. I said I was going to ask about targeted advertising, and one of the reasons I think the pendulum has swung back so sharply is a reaction to what you might call identity politics. In the book, you say that identity politics as we know it is made possible by computer-run sorting and targeting. The algorithms on these platforms will put us all together, and then we will say, “Here’s an identity. We’re a bloc. We have some political power as a bloc. Deal with us.” That seems true. I think we’ve all had that experience. We’ve seen that play out both in the culture, in our politics more broadly, but you can push back on that. You can say, “No, we don’t like that. Identity politics bad. That’s too woke,” and you can see the culture react to that. You can certainly see politicians and billionaires react to that. But I don’t think identity politics is only a product of quantifiability, of computer-aided targeting and sorting. It certainly existed before. Do you think the identity politics of today is defined by the fact that we all exist on platforms, or do you think it’s just shaped by it? What’s the relationship there? I remember being quite struck reading an article from 1968 in a magazine that I think was called Science and Technology, a popular magazine, like the Wired of the 1960s, by this guy, Ithiel de Sola Pool, who was an MIT political scientist.. In 1968, he was asked [alongside] JCR Licklider, the inventor of the internet, to speculate on what the computer revolution would mean by the year 2000. They were both really smart guys and they had really, really fascinating things to say. Ithiel de Sola Pool, this political scientist, said, “Certainly by then there will be personal newspapers. You will log onto your computer in the morning, and it will be networked,” because the computer was moving in 1968 from being a storage and data processing device to being a communications device, being both of those things. So he said, “You will be able to log onto your computer in the morning and be a personal computer.” And Pool said, “There really won’t be able to be party politics if you have your own newspaper because a political party is the organization of political dissent, of shared political priorities. I don’t think we’ll even have interest group politics,” like the Black Congressional Caucus or the Corn Farmers Association. “I don’t think we’ll even have that. We’ll really only be able to have personal politics. I just think that our notion of a representative government where we agree to elect people to represent not my individual interests, but the interests of my community, we won’t be able to do that because no one will have a sense of what is in the interest of their community. You’ll only have the sense of your own interests, and that’s not how a representative democracy works. Our system of government will be incompatible with our technology of communication.” Smart people saw this 50-60 years ago, and I think smart people see it now happening all the time. It’s something that is complicated for political campaigns to work with. You read interviews now with campaign consultants who say, “I really do not want to use these tools. I really do not want to do micro-targeted messaging, voter by voter, with deep-fake AI ads to convince people to vote for my candidate. I really believe in my candidate, but I don’t want to use these tools. But I have to use these tools because there’s no moratorium on using these tools, and therefore, I have to use the tools that I think my enemy will also use.” It’s a sad moment. I don’t think there’s anybody — well, I don’t know, there are probably some wretched human beings out there really excited to do deep-fakes and win elections that way, but most people in politics are not loving this moment. I said I was going to ask about targeted advertising, and I started with identity politics for a reason. If I look at how money on the internet is made broadly today, it is targeted advertising. I’m just thinking about your line about identity politics and how it’s made possible by computer-run sorting and targeting. Computer-run sorting and targeting is advertising. That is the modern advertising industry at scale. “We will find you, the person who is most susceptible to whatever advertising message we have, we might know so much about you that we can target that message even more tightly to you in an automated way, and we will deliver it to you.” The big tech companies have all gotten in trouble for over-sorting people. Meta got sued for creating ad categories that were protected classes by race and gender. Other platforms have gotten in trouble for not delivering housing advertisements to certain groups that were supposed to receive them or otherwise were discriminated against. You see this play out over and over again that there’s all kinds of sorting we’re not supposed to do, that we’ve actually made illegal. The algorithms don’t know this, the platforms maybe want to ignore it, and their entire model is delivering the right message to you at the right time so that you might buy something. Whether that is a foam mattress that you’ll pay for as a direct-to-consumer or whether it’s a political candidate, that’s the business we’re in. I’m wondering how you see that connecting to the artificial state. We’re going to measure everybody, quantify everybody, we’ll do capitalism at scale, and now we’re going to subsume our politics into it. Because you’re saying that the politicians themselves understand that maybe they shouldn’t do that. It’s helpful to remember that that’s not an invention of the internet or the personal computer era, or certainly not of the artificial intelligence era. There is a great book by my colleague, Liz Cohen, Consumers’ Republic, that argues that the consumer replaced the citizen as the individual entity of consequence in the United States in the 1950s, in the postwar era with the peacetime conversion of wartime factories. Consumption was what was going to save the country and advance the country’s interests, and American growth and American strength was associated with consumerism. In my lifetime, that’s been the way that we live. That’s not where the country was founded, and that’s also not inevitable. But the system that you’re describing with targeted advertising, which is effectively what the internet currently is, I actually don’t think that’s going to last. We’re not acting online primarily as citizens. Certainly I don’t feel that I am. I’m chiefly acting online as a consumer. I remember the day that I noticed that. In like 2000 I had a baby, and Google started sending me ads for breast pumps. I said, “Fuck this.” Remember when you were outraged by that and you say, “I hate that they know that I had a baby. That makes me mad. I didn’t tell them that”? But now we just accept it.. Everyone’s phones are listening to them and it’s whatever. Everyone’s phones are listening to them. You’re getting on a flight, you know that someone’s going to offer you Dramamine online. But that seemed, to a lot of people, inevitable and almost natural because the consumers’ republic is how we’ve lived for such a long time. I’m not trying to offer up a Luddite or nostalgic reading here, but when you walk down a city street, there’s City Hall and there’s the post office, and — this is going to make me sound like I’m 112 years old — there’s the JCPenney and the Walgreens. There are different places. It’s now just the one place where the information that City Hall might have about you or the information you might wish to share at City Hall, your house has been reappraised and you want to question that, or you’ve got a parking ticket and you want to appeal it, those were in one place. And then if you’re going to go buy ibuprofen or new socks, that was a different place. It’s now all corporatized and privatized. But the privatization of the public square is a transformation that is a long time coming. I’d be very curious to hear what you think about this, but the people that I read increasingly say the internet is just going to be for bots in fairly short order and the humans aren’t really going to be on it. It’s just going to be agentic AI doing your stuff. It’s really just going to be machines talking to machines, which is in a way what people thought it was going to be to begin with. I think that actually offers some prospect for restoring the real world as a distinctive place for how we engage with one another as families, communities, and governments. But where we are now, if this continues, I don’t see how democracy endures the corporatization of all public discourse. We have had many, many, many tech CEOs on the show and we have asked them very directly, “What happens when no one uses your app anymore, when it’s just the bots and the agents doing my bidding, and all of your business model has to fall away, and you are just a provider of Toyota Camrys?” Yeah, yeah! What do they say? What do they say?! It breaks down in two ways. Anybody who offers a physical service says, “Yeah, it was really hard to build this business. Go ahead and try to disrupt me with your bots. You won’t.”The CEO of Zocdoc, the CEO of Uber, and the CEO of TaskRabbit all say, “Yeah, go ahead and try. Try to find an army of people to come hang up your TV on demand. That’s our database, that’s our labor supply, and we will not be disrupted, because you can’t replace us.” Anybody who runs a virtual business or something that’s more software is freaking out. Amazon is basically freaking out. They’re a front end to a bunch of drop-shippers. They can be replaced. They’re the ones suing Perplexity. And Perplexity is saying, “Our software is the new labor, and you’re discriminating against our labor,” which I’m still trying to puzzle out. Do I believe that the agentic AI is equivalent to my labor? Should it have the same rights as me? That is an open question that I think the internet is not quite ready for, but it seems like the bleeding edge of what it actually means to even have an internet. If I can deploy bots out onto the internet on my behalf, should they have the same rights as I do, or do you actually need me and all the friction that I come with in order to build a business model, and do you have a right to that business model? I’m wondering if you know the answer, because that’d be great for me. I could just skip to the end. Yeah, I totally don’t know the answer. I’m fascinated by every time I look at the height of the tidal wave of the coming techlash, it’s higher and higher. I don’t see that manifesting itself in an effective way, but we’re in for really bumpy times. The other piece of it that strikes me is all of “the internet will go away” is wishful thinking on a part of the companies. They want this internet to go away. The economics of this internet are really well-known to them. There are a bunch of gatekeepers that just extract fees at every turn of this internet. Most famously there’s Apple. I think Elon Musk and Mark Zuckerberg and a whole bunch of other people would like to have business models that are not restricted by the iOS App Store and Apple’s 30 percent fees and however they feel about privacy. Saying, “We can build a new internet that’s all bots,” gets you away from the iPhone, gets you away from this device where Apple gets to decide what the internet is for in big and meaningful ways. But I think people like Instagram, and I don’t think they’re going to give up their phones. That keeps you in a world where there’s at least something happening, where you’re looking for other people in some way. And that to me is maybe the heart of the solution. I’ll connect it to the fact that you’re a college professor. You’re at the height of the techlash, as you just said. I’m watching college students boo AI at graduation ceremony after graduation ceremony and talk about it on the social platforms in big and meaningful ways. That seems like if there’s any kind of market pushback that leads to a political pushback that leads to actual change, that’s where it comes from, and that still came from the internet itself. No, it came from those people in a quad sweating in their stupid caps and gowns making a lot of noise together. It came from an actual group of humans in physical space together. I wouldn’t look to college or public school administrations to be of any help because they’re all just saying, “Oh, we made a deal with OpenAI. Here’s your not-so-free tool you have to use now.” Institutions, not just individuals, have to have positions of moral integrity in this moment, and I don’t see a ton of evidence of that. You see it maybe in the publishing industry, it’s very self-interested, and I think you see it in some state governments and some local governments, but I don’t think you see it in big law firms, big universities. I gave these lectures at Yale last year that are the basis for this book on the artificial state and had a lot of group meetings with Yale students. I had been told by a colleague that at the very first meeting of the AI task force, which the faculty thought was going to be about what our pedagogical position should be about — [was instead about] “We’re going to use this task force to deliberate on what’s the proper time and place for using these incredibly powerful tools, and then what places are maybe not good places.” He said, “The first meeting of the task force was about how we can brand AI at Yale so that it’s really sexy and people are excited about it. Are we going to call it YaAI? What’s the branding strategy here?” The faculty said, “What are you actually talking about? You brought us here to have a branding conversation?” I’m in a lecture hall with this wonderful group of students. I said, “Let’s just have a good discussion now. What about just having there be a two-week moratorium starting tomorrow? The president of the university could announce it tonight that, for two weeks, every class on campus is going to be a discussion section involving staff, faculty, and students on what our community policy should be about using this tool this year.” The students said, “Let’s do that. Why can’t we do that? Why can’t we have a discussion about it?” The staff and the faculty said, “Why are we not doing that?” You say, “Why are we not doing that?” That’s why the students are mad. They’re paying all this money, taking on all this debt, working their asses off to be replaced by machines and have no capacity, be granted no fulfillment of the role of student, scholar, citizen, member of a community, and what that means and should mean. It’s such a mismatch of the Silicon Valley rhetoric of the future of humanity. “This is bigger than the wheel or the invention of fire,” [against] like, “But we don’t give a shit what you think or want.” That’s what gives me hope, that restlessness around that. There was a resounding applause around this idea, and you will notice this is not what Yale did. Yale instead branded its relationship with OpenAI, and now it’s a corporate agreement. Let me connect that sense, that lack of agency that you’re describing, to what we see in our politics writ large. I think a lot of people are going to their local town/community planning meetings where a data center is being proposed. They’re saying no, and then it’s happening anyway. We see this playing out. Little “D” democratic politics are failing people in obvious ways. “Here’s this data center that you don’t want, and you’ve literally come to the meeting to register your opposition. Well, we’re doing it anyway because the town needs the jobs,” or whatever excuse is being put forward. We see this maybe most notably in Utah. Kevin O’Leary is going to build a data center no matter how much those people in Utah want it or not. And maybe the elected officials get thrown out because they said yes, and that will be the mechanism of change there. But actually, the representatives are not doing what the people want. The people feel this lack of agency. Your entire book is about the decaying of the liberal nation state. I could point to that very tiny thing. People don’t feel agency about data centers, and say, “That’s the tip of the spear. That’s what’s going to break it wide open.” If you don’t believe in your local government and you haven’t believed in your national or state government for a long time, what’s left? Is that recoverable? The thing that I’m worried about the most is maybe that’s not recoverable. If you can’t even keep the data center from showing up in your backyard, what else is there to believe in? If you can’t even get Yale to take a beat and talk to you, what else is there? Yeah. I don’t know, man. That is really grim. No, no, you’re supposed to depress me. It’s the other way around. [Laughs] I love that people are showing up and having those arguments. And if you were a smart community development board, you’d get ahead of that and say, “There are some good arguments for this data center that are honest arguments, and then there are some real arguments against it. Let’s have an open forum, and let’s see what the people think. And let’s also educate ourselves and the community,” because there’s a lot of dumbass stuff out there about data centers, I’m sure, certainly on both sides. I don’t know. I think the fact that that’s happening and is likely to really influence these elections is meaningful. There are political consequences for just going along to get along. But it’s part of a much bigger problem with money and American politics and the relationship between corporations and government, so there’s no really easy fix for that. To your question, structurally, is there any going back? My last book was about the history of the US Constitution. And one of the claims I make in this book is that it’s a problem for American politics and government when the Constitution becomes unamendable. The US Constitution hasn’t been meaningfully amended since 1971. Instead, the Supreme Court amends the Constitution in how it acts. So the longer that goes on, the more resentful people are of the Supreme Court. When people ask, “Would we ever get that back?” the example I often give is jury service. One thing that people really believe in is jury duty. Even if they don’t like to do it, they believe in it. They think it’s a good thing to have, that it involves fairness in our criminal justice system. Even if, objectively, juries often make the wrong decision, people believe it’s good that we are asked to go to a room with strangers and deliberate over what’s true and what’s not true. But imagine that, for some reason, jury service was abolished in 1971. And now in 2026, someone said, “You know what would actually be good would be bringing back jury duty, and having 12 random people decide whether or not your kid is guilty of aggravated assault.” There’s no way we would bring it back because trust in one another in civil society has so evaporated. That’s what’s worrying about the decay of people’s sense of, “We live in a representative government. If the majority of us don’t want this thing and we tell our elected officials we don’t want this thing, then we’re not going to have it.” And then when you repeatedly find out that you are going to have it in spite of what you want, your ability to believe in how the system works has really deteriorated. A lot of that sapping away of our civic strength and our capacity as citizens to deliberate with one another and hear one another out is because of the incursions of the artificial state. I want to end by asking about a phenomenon that I see more and more, especially after AI got booed at all the college graduations. It’s amazing. Between that and the data center pushback, it seems like the industry has decided that they need a new tack. They need to communicate more. OpenAI is just running around and its executives are like, “We have a marketing problem. We just need to market it better.” Google’s CEO was on the show, and he said, “I don’t think it’s a marketing problem. We actually have to prove that the products are useful to people.” That’s what the Microsoft CEO says. There’s a range of opinions here. The thing that all of them have started saying over and over and over again is that the democratic process should be trusted to put the guardrails on them. The CEO of Skydio was on. He is a drone maker. He supplies drones to the military and various governments, and he will tell you it’s as much power companies as the police, but don’t worry about the police. The democratic process is going to stop the police from infringing on your rights with drones. Maybe. I hear it with Anthropic, which just proposed a federal regulator for AI that will determine who runs the frontier models and do safety checks on them, and that’s the democratic process. I could probably make a list of every big tech executive at some point saying, “Democracy will stop us. We trust democracy.” Your entire book is about technology fraying democracy to its very core. Is this just self-serving on their part? Now that they’ve broken it, they’re saying, “That’s the thing that will stop us,” and they know that it won’t. Or is this actually the moment for democracy to reassert itself because they’re asking for it? Yes to both. It is self-serving on their part, and this goes pretty far back. Some years ago, OpenAI had this whole democratic inputs project where they’re going to get democratic inputs on how AI should run. This is where Claude’s constitution comes from. “We’re going to have a collective constitution. We’re going to crowdsource constitutional drafting.” The individuals involved in the democratic inputs project for OpenAI and the collective constitutional project for Anthropic really cared about those things. They knew nothing about the political process. They knew nothing about representative democracy, nor did they care to learn. The way collective constitutionalism worked, the democratic inputs project worked was basically just turning people into data points. “We’ll do hyper-scaling. Every American will be able to point and click and vote.” That’s not deliberative democracy. Actually, people have to be in a room together. They need to talk to one another. There needs to be a process. There need to be rules. There needs to be a parliamentarian. There need to be votes. There need to be rules about vetoing votes. There need to be rules about speech and process. So when they talk about, “Democracy will save us,” what they mean by democracy is something that I think, for most political scientists, is unrecognizable as a democratic process. It’s a buzzword for them. It’s been convenient for them at different moments in their recent past, and it seems convenient now. That said, that doesn’t mean this isn’t a moment that people who care about involving ordinary people in discussions around, “What do we want? What would be right? I ought to learn a little bit more about this, and I want to talk to some people, and I want to hear what my neighbors think. And I want to sit down with the town council, the neighborhood council and work it out.” That is the chief argument in my book. That can still happen. That should still happen, and I think it has to still happen. That seems like the next step. It seems like getting the college kids together to boo is maybe the thing that will solve democracy. As a college student who booed the Iraq War, I still want to believe this, whether or not that went my way. Dr. Lepore, this has been amazing. Thank you so much. A lot of fun. Thanks so much for having me. Questions or comments? Hit us up at decoder@theverge.com. We really do read every email!

Four Apple Stores in the U.S. Are Moving This Month
articles.description: Four of Apple's retail stores in the U.S. are moving this month, although all of them will only be a short distance from their existing locations. Apple Queens Center in Elmhurst, New York already moved to a temporary location in the shopping mall on Friday, July 17 while the existing store is remodeled. Apple did not indicate when the existing store will reopen. Apple Renaissance at Colony Park in Ridgeland, Mississippi is moving to a new spot within the same shopping center on Friday, July 24 at 10 a.m. local time. Apple's new storefront will be located right in front of the Show Fountain. Apple Briarwood in Ann Arbor, Michigan will be relocating to a new space at the mall on Friday, July 31 at 10 a.m. local time. The entrance to the new, larger store will be in front of The Lawn, a new outdoor space at the mall. Apple The Promenade Shops at Briargate in Colorado Springs, Colorado is moving six doors down to the left. The AirPods Max 2 are down to their second-best price
articles.description: There are a ton of deals available to shop today thanks to Best Buy’s “Black Friday in July” sale lasting all week. The sale typically aligns closely with Prime Day each year, but of course, Amazon’s shopping holiday happened much earlier than we expected. So it’s nice to have some deals in July. One of example of a great deal is Apple’s AirPods Max 2, which are down to $449.99 at Amazon and Best Buy, $100 off their usual price. It’s only the second time they’ve been discounted. Prime Day knocked them all the way down to $399.99, but today’s price isn’t bad at all if you missed out last month. They’re available at this price in every color. Apple AirPods Max (second-gen) Where to Buy: $549 $449 at Amazon $549 $449 at Best Buy Our review called the Max 2 a “great sequel, but not an ambitious one.” In short, not much has changed, especially in terms of design. There are some internal improvements that might make it worth it for those who have the original iteration (especially if you have the model with the Lightning connector). The Max 2 features USB-C connectivity like the 2024 revision, but has a built-in amp that delivers incredible sound that edges out the competition, not to mention the H2 wireless chip that enables features like live translation, adaptive audio, and conversation awareness. Some other great Verge-approved deals The Logitech G Pro X2 Superstrike wireless gaming mouse is a fascinating PC gaming accessory. Instead of having physical switches under its two main mouse buttons, it uses haptic motors to simulate the click sensation. The company made the switch to decrease latency, and to let you customize how much of a jolt each click delivers. If that sounds interesting to you, read our coverage, and consider picking it up at its first-ever discount at Amazon. The $179.99 mouse is down to $125.99, a temporary price cut that’ll be reflected at the checkout screen. Some other great Apple deals switched on overnight, including a four-pack of AirTags (second-gen) Bluetooth trackers. Originally $99.99, the four-pack is down to $89.99 at Amazon and Best Buy. Costco members can get an even better deal with five second-gen AirTags for $99.99. The latest AirTags’ biggest features include a louder alarm and extended range, which could give you a better chance at finding your lost items compared to the first-gen version, even if it’s four floors below (something the original AirTag couldn’t reliably do). Read Victoria Song’s review. Kodak’s Charmera isn’t a great camera. Let’s get that out of the way first. However, the name is on point — it’s charming as heck. The quality of the photos isn’t what you should buy it for. It’s just fun to have a flash-ready, screen-equipped digital camera connected to your keychain. Each Charmera comes in a blind box, so you won’t know which design you’ll get until you open it. articles.title: 韩国杠杆去到哪了：4大观测指标
articles.description: 有关本轮韩国股市杠杆资金的去化程度，我们从四个维度进行观测： ①融资余额：对比前几次去杠杆过程中融资余额最大下滑幅度来看，当前出清过程尚未过半。截至7/16，韩股融资余额为33.36万亿韩元，占韩股市值的比重为0.57%。本轮融资余额自最高点已下滑13.6%，去杠杆速度快于18年和22年熊市，慢于08年次贷危机，若对比此前几次去杠杆时期中融资余额最大下滑幅度来看(30%~70%)，当前杠杆出清的过程尚未过半。 ②散户经纪商保证余额：下滑至2月初以来较低水平。截至7/16，散户经纪商保证余额下滑28.7万亿韩元至108.1万亿韩元，为今年2月初以来较低水平，对应散户承接能力已显著回落。 ③强平规模：近期较此前高点显著回落。7.13-7.16，韩国强平规模为100-400亿韩元左右，占未缴纳保证金的比例降至4%以下，较此前1400亿/10%的高点明显回落。 ④杠杆ETF规模：显著回落，但几乎完全由净值回落贡献，多数ETF份额反而逆势抬升。截至7/16，韩国相关的前十大杠杠ETF的AUM由430亿美元回落至250亿美元，杠杆敞口占韩国市值的比重由2.1%降至1.6%。据测算，每5%的股价波动所引发的做市商再平衡资金流，占韩国过去一个月日均成交额比重，由17%降至11%。但值得注意的是，本轮规模回落几乎完全由净值贡献，多数杠杆ETF的份额逆势抬升，在韩国市场调整阶段中，这十大杠杆ETF录得近60亿美元的净流入。 四大维度中，结合市值占比、成交占比和净流入贡献来看，我们认为杠杆ETF是最核心的观测指标，其AUM变化和韩股波动率高度正相关。杠杆ETF规模回落至4月初的水平或负债端转为持续流出，可以被解读为杠杆压力的出清。 综合而言，当前资金面的一些积极信号包括：1）前十大杠杆ETF的规模较高点接近下滑超40%，对应股价波动引发的做市商Gamma hedge的影响降低，尤其是对SK海力士而言；2）韩国本土的三星电子杠杆ETF本周前三个交易日持续遭散户赎回；3）韩国散户保证金余额已出现企稳迹象；4）外资从此前的单边流出转为阶段性流入，高盛PB数据也显示对冲基金近期有所回流，历史经验表明外资的回流往往对应行情向上的拐点。 本文来源：兴证策略张启尧团队 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。

articles.title: AI云厂商向上延伸，GMI Cloud加码Agent生产化
articles.description: AI云厂商展示的产品，正在从GPU算力进一步延伸至模型调用和智能体部署。 7月17日至20日举行的2026世界人工智能大会（WAIC）上，AI云服务商GMI Cloud集中展示了AI Cloud、Cluster Engine、Inference Engine和AgentBox等产品，覆盖GPU资源、算力调度、模型推理及AI Agent部署等环节。 这套产品组合背后是AI企业对云基础设施需求的变化。 过去，企业采购AI云服务，首先关注的是能否获得足够的GPU。随着大模型逐渐进入实际业务，企业还需要处理算力资源调度、多模型接入、高并发运行以及应用部署等问题。 GMI Cloud试图将这些环节连接起来。 底层的AI Cloud主要负责提供GPU资源。作为Reference Platform NVIDIA Cloud Partner之一，GMI Cloud提供英伟达H100、H200、B200、GB200和GB300等GPU资源，主要用于模型训练、微调和生产级推理。 在GPU资源之上，GMI Cloud此次还展示了Cluster Engine，这是一套面向AI工作负载的算力管理平台，主要解决的是GPU资源如何被有效使用的问题。 对AI企业而言，算力成本不仅取决于GPU单价，也与资源利用率、任务排队时间和集群稳定性有关。模型推理流量通常存在明显波动，固定配置大量GPU容易造成闲置，仅在业务高峰临时扩容又可能影响响应速度。 集群调度平台就此成为AI云厂商向上延伸的一层能力。 GMI Cloud在此次WAIC上重点展示的另一项产品是AgentBox，这是一套面向生产级AI Agent的部署、运行和分发平台，内置了内置 MaaS模型库，通过单一API 密钥即可无缝调用170+全球顶尖大模型。 此次展出的产品反映出AI云市场正在发生的变化。 随着单纯获取GPU不再是企业面临的唯一问题，AI云厂商也开始从资源供应商向模型和应用层延伸。 对GMI Cloud而言，GPU仍然是产品体系的基础，但业务边界已经扩展至推理和Agent运行。AI云厂商未来竞争的重点，可能不只是拥有多少算力，还包括能否帮助企业把模型和智能体稳定地部署到真实业务中。 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。

articles.title: Apple Likely Left Jony Ive Out of Its OpenAI Lawsuit on Purpose
articles.description: Bloomberg's Mark Gurman says Apple's decision not to name its former design chief Jony Ive in its trade-secret lawsuit against OpenAI was likely a deliberate one, shaped in part by the company's relationship with Laurene Powell Jobs. Apple's roughly 40-page complaint refers only to unnamed "former Apple leaders" rather than calling out Ive, even though he leads design on OpenAI's hardware lineup through his firm LoveFrom, built on the back of OpenAI's $6.5 billion acquisition of his startup io Products. The allegations instead center on former iPhone executive Tang Tan, now OpenAI's chief hardware officer, whom Apple accuses of coaching recruits to bypass security measures and bring Apple hardware into interviews for "show-and-tell" sessions. "Power On" newsletter, Gurman notes that Apple's decision likely reflects, at least in part, a genuine absence of evidence against Ive, who is reportedly not closely involved in OpenAI's day-to-day recruiting or engineering. He argues, however, that the relationship between Powell Jobs and Ive was also a significant factor. The two are described as close friends, with Ive having delivered a tribute at Steve Jobs' memorial service in 2011. Powell Jobs was an investor in io Products and remains a supporter of LoveFrom. According to Gurman, naming Ive in the complaint risked straining Apple's relationship with a figure who continues to carry considerable influence within the company. Tim Cook and his successor John Ternus. He characterizes her placement as a visible show of support for Apple's leadership transition. 400 former Apple employees are now reported to work at OpenAI, whose first hardware product is expected to be a portable smart speaker aimed at competing with the iPhone in the long term. articles.description: IT之家 7 月 20 日消息，据 The Information 报道，知情人士透露，谷歌正在研发一款代号为“Frozen v2”的全新服务器芯片，该芯片的核心突破在于将 Gemini 大模型的底层运算架构直接固化进硬件层面，从而大幅降低 AI 推理过程中的能耗与延迟，单位功耗可处理的词元数量预计达到谷歌现有自研 AI 芯片的 6 至 10 倍。 谷歌当前正面临严峻的 AI 算力短缺困境。内部资源紧张已导致谷歌云不得不回绝部分外部客户的合作订单。Frozen v2 项目的启动，正是为了从根本上破解这一瓶颈。知情人士表示，该芯片最早计划于 2028 年部署。 IT之家注意到，“Frozen”（冻结）这一代号精准概括了其设计哲学：将大模型的部分运算逻辑永久蚀刻在硅片硬件中。与英伟达 GPU 及谷歌 TPU 等通用型芯片不同，Frozen v2 并非通用芯片，而是专为 Gemini 系列模型量身打造的专用芯片。通用芯片在运行任意模型时需实时执行大量逻辑判断，而 Frozen v2 通过内置 Gemini 的底层运算逻辑，可显著减少运算步骤和数据搬运量，实现更快的用户响应速度，并有望支撑谷歌推出全新的 AI 应用场景。 Frozen v2 并非谷歌首次尝试将 AI 模型“写入”硬件。其初代方案由谷歌 DeepMind 首席科学家杰夫 · 迪恩（Jeff Dean）牵头，计划将完整的模型权重直接蚀刻进芯片。但该方案存在一个致命缺陷：芯片只能适配单一版本的 Gemini 模型，硬件生命周期极短，因此项目被搁置多年。 Frozen v2 在初代基础上进行了关键调整，不再固化完整模型权重，而是仅将底层架构逻辑固化进芯片，同时保留通过更新内置模型权重（决定模型回答质量的核心参数）进行迭代的能力。不过，这也意味着谷歌押注自身会持续沿用当前 Gemini 大模型的底层架构，只有后续迭代的 Gemini 模型沿用与芯片设计时一致的基础架构，才能在该芯片上正常运行。 目前，工程师团队仍在敲定核心功能模块及各组件的协同方案，同时在权衡固化模型信息的深度，以在硬件灵活性与运行能效之间取得最佳平衡。 Frozen v2 将开辟一条全新的自研芯片产品线，与谷歌现有的张量处理器（TPU）形成互补关系，而非取而代之。谷歌今年已推出第八代 TPU，并直接面向云客户推广，正面挑战英伟达在 AI 芯片市场的垄断地位。谷歌已与 Meta 签署数十亿美元大单，向其出租 TPU 算力，同时积极将 TPU 推向英伟达的核心云厂商客户。 值得注意的是，谷歌自研 AI 芯片的战略已初见成效。通过在设计 TPU 时围绕 Gemini 进行适配，谷歌已有效降低了 Gemini 模型的运行成本，只是 TPU 内置的模型信息远少于 Frozen 系列芯片。 尽管技术前景广阔，谷歌目前并无大规模量产 Frozen v2 的计划，其产能规模将远低于 TPU。知情人士透露，有限的量产规模使谷歌可以延后引入外部设计和代工合作伙伴。谷歌更将这一代产品视为技术试验平台，待大模型底层架构趋于稳定后，为研发更高专用化芯片积累工程经验。 谷歌官方发言人对此回应称，公司各团队“持续研发、测试各类创新技术，力求为用户与企业客户实现极致性能与能效”，并强调“并非所有研发项目都会落地量产，但这种全方位技术探索，是我们全栈自研技术路线的核心一环”。

消息称小鹏汽车 AI Infra 负责人陆思渊将离职，下一站是 OpenAI
articles.description: IT之家 7 月 20 日消息，据雷峰网新智驾消息，小鹏汽车 AI 基础架构部负责人陆思渊即将离职，目前正在进行工作交接。陆思渊的下一站已确定，将前往 OpenAI 参与具身智能机器人方向的研发工作。 报道称，陆思渊主要负责搭建小鹏汽车 AI Infra（IT之家注：AI 基础架构）体系，目前在小鹏直管约 200 人团队，其职责覆盖模型训练框架、GPU 集群管理、自研芯片编译器、数据、模型量化优化，以及车端推理部署与量产落地的完整链路。 与小鹏汽车多数竞争对手依赖英伟达等第三方芯片平台不同，小鹏选择自研芯片路线。知情人士指出，小鹏自研芯片配套的编译器与推理运行时系统必须由 AI Infra 团队完成，这是小鹏能够将端到端模型真正推向量产的关键前提。 据悉，小鹏目前还未找到可以代替陆思渊的合适人选，陆思渊离职后，他的团队预计将被拆分为三个以上独立团队，由不同负责人分别管理，最大程度降低陆思渊离任后的影响。

articles.description: IT之家 7 月 20 日消息，7 月 20 日，中国商飞公司参加 2026 年范堡罗国际航展，展出了 C909 基本型和衍生型飞机模型以及 C919、C929 飞机模型，呈现了中国商用飞机系列产品布局。 IT之家从官方介绍获悉，中国商飞公司持续丰富飞机产品谱系、推进系列化发展。90 座级的 C909 支线飞机对高温、高原、短窄跑道等运行环境具备良好的适应性，目前已交付十余家客户，主要在中国和东南亚地区投入商业运营。190 座级的 C919 单通道干线飞机已交付东航、国航、南航并投入商业运营。290 座级的 C929 宽体飞机设计工作正在稳步推进。在此基础上，中国商飞公司还推出了 C909 医疗机、灭火机、货机、公务机、应急救援指挥机。 目前，官方暂未公布 C929 宽体飞机的具体信息。作为参考，已经交付的 C919 大型客机是我国首款按照国际通行适航标准自行研制、具有自主知识产权的喷气式干线客机，座级 158-192 座，航程 4075-5555 公里。2015 年 11 月 2 日完成总装下线，2017 年 5 月 5 日成功首飞，2022 年 9 月 29 日获得中国民用航空局颁发的型号合格证，2022 年 12 月 9 日全球首架交付，2023 年 5 月 28 日圆满完成首次商业飞行。 据工信部今日最新透露，C919 大型客机累计交付 41 架、安全飞行时长突破 13 万小时。

元脑服务器：推出 CXL 内存跨代扩展方案，实现 DDR5 和 DDR4 同机部署内存扩容
articles.description: IT之家 7 月 20 日消息，元脑服务器今日宣布，推出 CXL（Compute Express Link）内存跨代扩展方案，实现 DDR5 和 DDR4 同机部署内存扩容。 官方表示，基于元脑服务器 NF5280，在 24 条本地 DDR5 内存基本配置下，通过自研 CXL 内存扩展卡，单机最多可扩展 16 条 DDR4 内存，按照单条内存 32GB 容量，额外扩展 512GB 内存，整机内存容量提升 33%，成本大幅降低 25%。 IT之家从官方获悉，目前该方案已在国内某大型互联网客户完成验证并实现规模应用。 据介绍，该方案结合元脑服务器操作系统 KOS 池化内存技术，将本地 DRAM 内存与 CXL 扩展内存融合为统一逻辑内存空间，通过冷热数据识别、动态迁移和 NUMA 感知调度策略，让扩展内存达到本地内存相当性能，提升 CPU 利用率 30%。 CXL 内存扩展卡采用标准 PCIe 5.0 x16 全高半长双宽设计，支持 CXL 2.0 协议，PCIe 插槽可提供 75W 功耗，外接独立 12V 供电后整卡最大功耗支持 150W。搭配 NF5280 服务器，单张 CXL 扩展卡可挂载 4 条 DDR4 内存，单机最多支持 4 张 CXL 扩展卡，按照单条 32GB DDR4 内存计算，整机可额外扩展 512GB 内存容量。 官方表示，以 1000 台的服务器集群计算，客户使用 CXL+DDR4 的内存跨代扩展方案，相较全部使用 DDR5 内存，能够大幅节省 1.2 亿元。

中概互联网巨头已触底？伯恩斯坦：AI成本被过度悲观解读，重点关注腾讯
articles.description: 中国互联网板块在经历上半年深度调整后，正迎来一轮情绪修复。 据追风交易台，伯恩斯坦最新研究报告认为，市场对AI推理成本的悲观解读已严重失真，叠加腾讯Hy3模型发布及阿里云增长超预期等催化剂，板块估值已从2022至2023年的历史低谷水平出现反弹，风险收益比有所改善。 腾讯Hy3模型的发布以及小微助手开始向用户推送，是近期板块情绪回暖的核心驱动力。 伯恩斯坦分析师Robin Zhu在报告中指出，此前市场流传的部分AI成本叙事——例如平台将需要无限期补贴推理成本——已属"严重失实且过度悲观"。与此同时，阿里云第二季度营收增速加速至40%中段区间，电商利润亦好于预期，共同推动了板块整体反弹。 伯恩斯坦维持腾讯、阿里巴巴、网易、京东及Boss直聘的"跑赢大市"评级。其中腾讯目标价780港元，对应当前股价约有69%的上行空间；京东目标价40美元，对应2026年预期市盈率仅约8.4倍。 报告明确指出，腾讯当前11至12倍的远期市盈率估值偏低，随着各项利空因素逐步消散，股价有望重新回归2021年以来17至18倍的历史均值区间。 AI成本恐慌被过度放大，推理费用并非无底洞 围绕腾讯和阿里巴巴的核心空头逻辑之一，在于AI推出将导致推理成本大幅侵蚀利润，而消费端AI变现却遥遥无期。 伯恩斯坦对此提出反驳：推理成本的爆发式增长，前提是代理式（agentic）交易量和GMV同步起飞。 从数据来看，聊天机器人式对话通常仅消耗数百个token，而代理式交易平均消耗约5万个token。换言之，腾讯的token消耗量只有在代理式交易量真正放量时才会呈指数级增长。 报告认为，用户参与度与变现增长之间存在时间差，但历史规律表明后者是"何时发生"而非"是否发生"的问题。 在资本开支层面，腾讯过去12个月资本开支占营收比例为10.9%，低于阿里巴巴的12.3%。 相对于经营现金流，腾讯的资本开支扩张空间远大于阿里巴巴。阿里云方面，第二季度营收增速加速至40%中段，低双位数的利润率意味着35%至40%的增量现金利润率，阿里巴巴亦表示年内将继续推进算力价格上调。 腾讯AI战略轮廓渐清，Hy4时间表成关键观察点 伯恩斯坦在报告中详细梳理了腾讯AI布局的最新进展。Hy3模型在4月预览版基础上取得显著提升，小微助手亦已开始向用户灰度推送，早期反馈积极，并与主要安卓手机厂商签署的agent2agent协议形成协同。 报告指出，腾讯Hy团队与微信团队此前保持独立运作，管理层解释称此举旨在避免相互依赖、防止一方延误拖累另一方。微信团队在此期间借助DeepSeek等中国前沿模型推进产品迭代，元宝及Workbuddy的月活用户已达800至900万，为Hy3团队提供了用户反馈来源。 伯恩斯坦预计，随着Hy4及后续模型性能持续提升，两个团队的协同设计程度将逐步加深。参照中国AI实验室参数规模平均扩大2至2.5倍的规律，Hy4预览版有望于年底前后发布。报告认为，腾讯在微信内希望实现的大多数AI功能，以现有代理式AI标准衡量相对直接，意味着自研模型将较快达到"足够好"的水平。 在变现路径上，报告特别强调，微信小程序数万亿人民币的GMV是腾讯AI变现的核心机遇，通过商家侧实现货币化。这与西方市场投资者已基本放弃消费端AI变现预期的悲观情绪形成鲜明对比。 阿里巴巴业务重组提振估值，季节性催化剂值得关注 伯恩斯坦对阿里巴巴近期的业务架构调整持审慎乐观态度。将盒马从"其他业务"并入中国电商板块、将平头哥芯片业务纳入云计算板块，将有助于提升投资者重点关注的业务分部增速，在分类加总估值（SOTP）框架下具有正面意义。 报告指出，Neocloud客户销售平头哥芯片并回租算力的安排，有助于降低阿里云报告口径的资本密集度，同时为外部芯片销售收入叙事提供支撑。此外，阿里巴巴持有约5%的长鑫科技股权，其潜在价值不容忽视。 历史规律同样值得关注：2024年和2025年，阿里巴巴股价均在9月云栖大会前后达到阶段性高点。伯恩斯坦认为，长鑫科技 IPO进展及云栖大会构成未来数月的重要催化剂窗口。 网易、京东及Boss直聘：低估值叠加盈利增长 在其他重点标的方面，伯恩斯坦对网易、京东和Boss直聘均持积极看法，核心逻辑在于估值偏低与盈利增长的组合。 网易方面，《燃魂》（Sea of Remnants）将于7月23日国内上线，报告预计股价届时可能出现一定回调，但下半年营收低基数、加速回购、南向资金纳入预期以及《Ananta》后续消息，构成较为清晰的催化剂路径。伯恩斯坦回测数据显示，过去10年网易回购加速与随后股价表现之间存在高度相关性。 京东和Boss直聘目前均以中个位数远期市盈率交易——后者剔除现金及投资后仅约4倍——而两家公司均维持两位数的盈利增长。伯恩斯坦上调了京东盈利预测，2026年非GAAP净利润预测较此前提升约8.8%，主要反映外卖业务亏损收窄快于预期及持续的利润率改善。 相比之下，报告对美团和拼多多态度较为谨慎。美团近期反弹后上行空间有限，且AI投入或仍处于早期阶段；拼多多管理层持续回避与投资者的资本回报沟通，被报告视为长期投资者面临的核心障碍。 估值仍接近历史低位，但修复条件正在积累 从整体估值来看，伯恩斯坦覆盖的中国互联网股票今年以来平均下跌约16%（含近期反弹），目前平均对应2026年和2027年预期市盈率分别为14.3倍和12.1倍，后者仅略高于2022至2023年的历史低点——彼时基本面受中国"清零"政策严重压制。 自由现金流/企业价值收益率方面，腾讯和京东约为5%，网易约为10%，Boss直聘接近20%。京东、Boss直聘和拼多多的净现金均超过市值的40%，其中京东和Boss直聘管理层已积极回购股票。 伯恩斯坦认为，腾讯当前低估值反映的是一系列"当下合理但终将消散"的担忧，包括游戏增长放缓及AI投入带来的费用压力。触发更明确反转信号的条件包括：经营利润预测触底回升、出现爆款新游戏（《三角洲行动》目前表现强劲），或Hy4发布真正平息AI能力争议。报告认为，随着上述因素逐步落地，腾讯股价不太可能长期停留在11至12倍远期市盈率的水平。 ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ As for new Mac Pro hardware, there were two additional models developed by Apple that never saw the light of day: J170 and J190. The former was a new Intel Corp. Mac Pro (yes, even when Apple was making its own silicon) to address certain uses. The latter was an M3 Ultra version that was supposed to launch alongside the M3 Ultra Mac Studio in early 2025. Gurman did not specify what "certain uses" the Intel model was meant to address, but its existence suggests Apple explored keeping an x86 option alive for specific professional workflows even years into the Apple silicon era. 科学家根据体细胞突变量化人类寿命的极限
articles.description: 体细胞突变随年龄增长而积累，能导致细胞死亡。根据发表在《npj Aging》期刊上的一项研究，科学家开发出一种方法量化体细胞突变对人类寿命的影响。研究只考虑体细胞突变，没有考虑其它任何衰老特征。研究发现，肝脏等增殖性组织通过细胞更新能在数千年内维持功能，而神经元和心肌细胞等有丝分裂后细胞则是长寿的重要瓶颈。综合多个器官预测的人类寿命中位数是 146-194 岁，约为目前人类寿命的两倍。这意味着体细胞突变是衰老的重要驱动因素，但无法单独解释目前的人类寿命，驱动衰老的还有其它因素。

articles.title: 'ClickLock' Malware Coerces Mac Users Into Giving Up Passwords
articles.description: Security firm Group-IB has identified a new piece of macOS malware in the wild that pressures users into surrendering their passwords via a barrage of fake system prompts. Dubbed "ClickLock Stealer," the malware needs no exploits and no elevated privileges to work. Instead, the attack depends on the victim pasting a command into Terminal and running it. The command then executes a script, and everything else follows. Group-IB did not directly observe how victims are lured into pasting the command, but based on the script's behavior, the firm believes it's served through a fake "ClickFix" page posing as a Cloudflare check or browser verification step. Such pages instruct visitors to copy a command and run it in Terminal as a supposed "verification requirement." Once it's up and running, the script discreetly downloads several modules and shows a terminal-based loading animation mimicking a Cloudflare progress bar with browser verification. If a user declines the initial password dialog that appears, the malware starts locking system usage. Specifically, the malware kills every visible app every 210 milliseconds while the password prompt remains on screen, and the rest of the desktop stays unusable until the victim gives in. Meanwhile, another loop suppresses macOS security notifications for roughly six hours. If the user gives up and enters their password, a second, genuine macOS prompt is subsequently forced to the front, asking them to allow access to a Keychain item. Granting it hands over Chrome's "Safe Storage" AES key, which is what the browser uses to encrypt saved passwords and cookies. With the login password and Chrome's encryption obtained, ClickLock then harvests browser credentials, Keychain data, password manager vaults, and any cryptocurrency wallets, and then sends it all to a Telegram bot. It also installs a hidden backdoor disguised as an iCloud process to give it continual access. Group-IB says the campaign has been active since May 2026 and has targeted at least 100 victims across 33 countries. More than half of the victims were in Europe. added a warning that appears when the user attempts to paste a command into Terminal from a website, chat, or message, and blocks the paste until the user reviews it. (Opera browser also recently added a similar feature.) articles.title: 调查显示：苹果产品涨价致超九成用户调整购买行为，超 1/3 将降低升级频率
articles.description: IT之家 7 月 20 日消息，一项针对数千名 9to5Mac 读者的调查显示，苹果产品价格上涨很可能会导致用户延长升级周期，即使是最忠实的苹果用户也难以完全不受影响。 在调查结果中，“降低升级频率”是读者选择最多的应对方式，而只有 9% 的受访者表示，涨价不会改变他们的购买行为。 苹果部分产品的价格涨幅已经超过 50%，在某些情况下，内存和存储容量升级的价格甚至翻了一倍。而目前的迹象显示，这种高价状态短期内并不会改善。 随后的一份分析师报告指出，供应链价格在 2028 年之前可能不会出现明显改善，即使到那时，改善幅度也可能非常有限。 这意味着，目前明显提高的苹果产品售价至少可能持续数年，甚至未来也不一定会完全恢复到过去的水平。 但调查显示，即使是高度关注苹果产品的用户，也存在明显的承受极限。超过 90% 的受访者表示，他们会因为价格上涨而调整购买行为，其中超过三分之一的人表示会减少升级频率。 IT之家附调查结果如下： 降低升级频率：38% 等待促销降价：14% 放弃购买一款或多款苹果产品：12% 选择更低端型号：9% 不会受到影响：9% 一位读者留言表示：“我仍然会购买苹果产品。但我可能不会每年升级手机，也不会每三年升级一次电脑。我可能会改成每两到三年升级一次手机，每五到六年升级一次电脑。” 当然，未来如果苹果推出足够有吸引力的新功能，也可能重新改变消费者的决定。 不过，这项调查至少表明，苹果可能需要面对销量增长放缓的风险，而如果市场需求受到影响，这或许会促使苹果未来采取某种形式的降价策略，以维持消费者购买意愿。

articles.description: 黄金市场多空博弈进入关键阶段。技术面显示下行压力犹存，但央行购金需求持续强劲，多方机构对黄金中期走势判断出现明显分歧。 美银（BofA）最新分析指出，黄金目前处于下行通道，"死亡交叉"信号暗示进一步下跌空间，但TD序列指标显示价格或将转向。该行认为，本轮调整仅持续24周，相较于此前长达121周的上升趋势，修正周期可能尚未结束，并将3500美元区间视为关键支撑位。 与此同时，高盛预计央行5月购金量达81吨，认为央行购金将为金价提供价格底部支撑，抵消美联储鹰派预期带来的短期下行压力。 技术信号偏弱，3500美元或成关键防线 美银最新技术分析显示，黄金目前仍处于下行通道中，“死亡交叉”形态已经形成，短期技术面偏向继续承压。不过，该行同时指出，TD序列指标已释放潜在反转信号，意味着金价或接近阶段性调整窗口，空头力量并非完全占据主导。 美银表示，自2000年以来，黄金长期运行中的通道线一直是重要技术枢纽。目前来看，支撑区域正逐步向3500美元附近移动。该行认为，本轮调整周期仍可能没有结束。相比此前持续约121周的上涨趋势，当前回调仅持续约24周，修正时间可能仍有延续空间，金价在确认中期底部前或继续维持震荡走势。 来源：美国银行 央行购金成重要支撑 尽管技术面偏弱，但央行持续购金正在成为黄金市场的重要支撑力量。高盛最新模型显示，全球央行5月购金量预计达到81吨，按三个月季节性调整后的月均水平计算约为67吨，明显高于2022年前约17吨的历史平均水平。 高盛指出，近期央行购金预测重新走强。该行认为，在美联储偏鹰派预期对金价形成短期压制的背景下，央行需求将为黄金提供重要的价格底部支撑。 法国巴黎银行则注意到，今年3月官方部门黄金持仓出现14个月以来首次净卖出。不过，该行认为这一变化更可能是短期异常现象，而非央行购金趋势逆转。 来源：GIR 资金情绪分化：期货看多，期权市场寻求保护 资金流向显示，黄金市场内部正在出现分歧。 美银数据显示，尽管黄金价格较2026年初高点回落，但期货市场净多头仓位占未平仓合约比例仍保持偏高水平。法国巴黎银行表示，黄金6月调整期间，基金投资者开始逢低买入，净投机多头持仓随后回升，显示部分资金仍押注黄金中长期上涨趋势。 但期权市场释放出更谨慎信号。该行指出，自3月以来，基金整体倾向于买入黄金看跌期权，表明投资者正在通过期权策略对冲下行风险，至少短期内市场对进一步上涨并不充分乐观。 来源：法国巴黎银行 通胀逻辑退潮，债务压力强化黄金长期配置价值 从宏观逻辑来看，法国巴黎银行认为，黄金传统的“通胀对冲”逻辑正在发生变化。 当前市场更关注高通胀预期可能推动利率维持高位，而非单纯将通胀本身视为黄金买入理由。这也解释了为何在能源价格上涨推升通胀预期、同时市场重新定价美联储政策路径期间，黄金反而承压。 不过，该行认为，美国财政状况正在成为黄金长期支撑因素。自2025年7月以来，美国公共债务规模已增加约3万亿美元，对美国债务可持续性的担忧可能持续推动投资者配置黄金。 此外，黄金与美股资产的相关性也出现变化。2024年至2025年大部分时间里，黄金与美股一度呈现正相关，但进入2026年后，两者相关性重新转负，黄金的避险属性正在资产配置中重新显现。 来源：法国巴黎银行 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。

articles.title: 不设价格区间增持！上海银行部分高管中层拟1500万元“抄底”
articles.description: 银行业的“信心”不止于来自银行本身，有时候也包括银行的员工。 7月20日晚间，上海银行发布公告称，公司部分董事、高级管理人员及中层干部，计划以自有资金通过交易所集中竞价交易方式增持公司A股股份，合计增持金额不低于1500万元。此次增持计划不设价格区间，实施期限为自2026年7月21日起6个月内。 这并非公司层面的融资或回购安排，而是管理层及中层干部以个人自有资金“入场”。在资本市场，这样的行动信号，有时候被市场视为比公司回购更积极的信号。 高管中层共同增持 根据公告，本次增持计划的实施主体为上海银行部分董事、高级管理人员及中层干部。 增持主体拟通过上海证券交易所交易系统，以集中竞价方式买入上海银行无限售条件流通A股股票，拟增持金额合计不低于人民币1500万元。 公告并未设置增持价格区间，这意味着增持主体将在计划期内结合市场情况实施买入。 从时间安排看，本次计划将于2026年7月21日起6个月内实施。若期间存在限制董事、高级管理人员买卖股票的N个交易日，实施期限将相应顺延。 员工“抄底”全部用自有资金 值得注意的是，本次增持所需资金均为增持主体的自有资金。上海银行在公告中明确表示，不存在因资金未能到位而导致增持计划无法实施的风险。 与此同时，参与此次计划的董事、高级管理人员及中层干部承诺，在增持计划实施期间以及法定期限内，不减持其持有的公司股份。这一安排进一步强化了增持行为的长期导向，也表明相关主体并非进行短期交易，而是以实际持股表达对公司价值的认可。 上海银行公告表示，此次增持的主要目的，是基于对公司未来发展前景的信心，以及对公司长期投资价值的认可。 “不设价格区间” 相较于设置明确价格上限的增持计划，本次上海银行增持安排未设价格区间。 换言之，对于他们的员工来说，在未来6个月里，可以自由选择买入时机。 市场人士通常认为，这类安排体现出增持主体更看重公司中长期价值，而非仅在某一特定价格水平进行交易。 上海银行表示，公司将持续关注本次增持主体买入公司A股股票的进展，并按照相关法律法规和监管要求及时履行信息披露义务。 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。

articles.description: 新易盛近日在电话会议上表示，整体来看，二季度业绩预告情况与公司年初对全年整体情况的预期基本吻合，利润增长的核心驱动力包括以下几方面：1. 订单层面：订单交付需求的增长，预计下半年订单交付情况仍处于快速增长阶段，行业景气度持续高位，Q3/Q4及明年的订单能见度较高；2. 供应链端：Q1供应链紧张的情况对交付造成一定影响，Q2起逐步缓解，Q3/Q4将趋于稳定，得益于公司前期针对核心原材料做了充分的备货与锁定安排；3. 汇兑影响：一季度汇兑损失对利润影响较为明显，二季度该影响幅度大幅收窄。（第一财经）

articles.title: 低空云层多年来为地球“遮阳降温”，但科学家预警这一趋势即将逆转
articles.description: IT之家 7 月 20 日消息，近年来，低空云层数量增加，为海洋遮挡阳光并帮助降低地球温度。但这一反馈机制如今可能正在发生逆转，并可能进一步加快全球变暖速度。 据IT之家了解，云层一直是预测未来气候变化过程中最大的“不确定因素”之一，因为它们反射太阳辐射的方式十分复杂，既可能让地球升温，也可能帮助降温。 位于对流层上部的薄薄卷云，由于无法大量反射进入地球的阳光，反而会阻挡地表向外释放的热量，因此具有增温作用。 相比之下，位于低层对流层的大面积层积云则会将阳光反射回太空，从而降低地球温度。这也是为什么地球工程研究人员曾尝试喷洒微小海水颗粒，希望制造更多、更明亮的反射性云层。 气候模型预测，随着全球气温升高，能够阻挡阳光的低空云层数量会减少。这可能启动一个导致进一步升温的正反馈循环：温度越高，低空云越少，太阳能量吸收越多，地球继续升温。 然而，过去的卫星数据一直不足以明确判断低空云层究竟是在增加还是减少，尤其是在东南太平洋和大西洋等区域，因为这些地方通常形成规模最大、持续时间最长的云层覆盖。 如今，来自美国哥伦比亚大学的 Gregory Cesana 和 Assia Arouf 首次估算了自 1979 年卫星观测时代开始以来的低空云覆盖变化情况。 两位研究人员首先将海表温度、风速、大气稳定性等数据，与现代卫星设备测量得到的低空云覆盖情况进行关联分析，然后利用这些关系，推算出过去几十年中卫星观测能力较弱时期的低空云覆盖变化。 研究发现，自 1979 年以来，低空云覆盖范围实际上一直在扩大，使地球表面反射出去的能量增加了每平方米 0.32 瓦。 作为对比，人类活动导致的气候变化目前正在以约每平方米 2.72 瓦的速度增加地球吸收的热量。这意味着低空云层抵消了一部分全球升温效应，不过目前还很难准确计算它究竟降低了多少温度。 “我们得到的是一种负反馈，也就是说，云层实际上正在抵抗变暖。”Cesana 表示，“而这与气候模型中那些理想化实验得到的结果完全不同。” 研究人员发现，在东太平洋等热带地区，低空云覆盖率每十年增加约 0.18%。原因在于，东太平洋升温速度低于许多气候模型此前预测的水平，而西太平洋则明显变暖。 因此，东太平洋上空的近地表空气仍然保持较低温度，而大气环流则不断将来自西太平洋的暖空气带到其上方。 这种形成的温度逆温层，会阻止温暖、干燥并正在下沉的空气与低层层积云混合。Cesana 解释说：“这将有利于低空云形成，或者让它们更加稳定，从而持续更长时间。” 低空云减少可能成为新的变暖加速因素 不过，科学家预计，东太平洋未来很快可能会开始升温。其中一个原因是，人类正在加强对硫污染的控制。硫污染会形成能够冷却地球的气溶胶云，同时影响大气和海洋环流。随着硫污染减少，温暖、下沉的空气可能会开始驱散部分低空云。 这一变化可能已经开始出现。今年 3 月，伦敦帝国理工学院的 Paulo Ceppi 及其同事发现，自 2003 年以来，全球低空云覆盖率一直在下降。 另一项发表于 2024 年的研究则指出，近年来全球变暖速度加快，可能部分源于低空云正开始产生增强型正反馈效应。 Ceppi 表示：“没有理由认为我们高估了未来气候变化的影响。事实上，由于云层对全球变暖的放大作用，我们可能反而略微低估了未来气候变化的影响。” Cesana 认为，低空云覆盖增加这一发现实际上可能是一个坏消息。原因在于，如果这一趋势按照预期发生逆转，原本被云层遮挡的变暖效应可能会被“释放”，从而进一步加速气候变化。他说：“像目前正在东太平洋形成的厄尔尼诺事件，会减少低空云层，因此我们将提前感受到未来可能发生的情况。”

articles.title: 高盛：美国通胀正从局部走向全面扩散，但远未重演2022年危机
articles.description: 美国通胀扩散风险正在成为现实，但程度远未达到危机水平。 高盛经济学家Jessica Rindels的最新研究显示，以美联储首选通胀指标个人消费支出（PCE）衡量，当前通胀广度已高于1990年至2019年的历史均值，尤其在加权口径下表现突出。这一结论与新任美联储主席沃什上周国会听证时的担忧形成呼应——沃什明确将防止个别价格上涨"全面扩散"列为首要职责之一。 然而，Rindels的研究同时提供了一个重要的参照坐标：在0至10的自定义量化尺度上（0对应1990至2019年均值，10对应2022年通胀峰值），当前加权口径下的通胀广度读数为6，未加权口径仅为2，均远低于疫情期间的极端水平。市场对此反应相对平静，标普500期货周一盘前上涨约22个基点。 量化框架：通胀扩散程度如何衡量 Rindels采用三重过滤方法构建分析框架： 以PCE作为基础数据来源，采用六个月年化变动率平滑短期波动，并分别按各分项在PCE中的权重（加权）和逐类别等权处理（未加权）两种口径进行统计。 在此框架下，通胀广度被定义为PCE各分项中涨幅超过3%的类别占比。加权口径读数为6，意味着按消费权重计算，当前通胀扩散程度已接近2022年峰值的六成；而未加权口径读数仅为2，说明价格上涨在类别数量上仍相对集中，并未全面铺开。 两种口径之间的显著差异表明，当前通胀压力主要集中在权重较大的消费类别，而非均匀分布于各个细分领域。 价格上涨集中于视听、金融、医疗与交通 Rindels的研究指出，当前价格涨幅最快的领域集中在视频/音频服务、金融服务、医疗服务以及机票/交通运输四大类别。 这些类别在PCE中权重较高，是推动加权口径读数偏高的主要来源。 相比之下，住房租金虽仍是通胀的重要构成部分，但Rindels预测其影响将逐步消退——预计今年第四季度，住房租金涨幅将回落至3%以下，届时对整体通胀广度的拉动作用将明显减弱。这一预判为市场提供了一定的前景缓释信号。 市场定价：降息预期降温，9月加息概率升至逾五成 沃什上周的国会听证被市场普遍解读为偏鹰派基调。 此后，美国2年期国债收益率从接近4.3%的水平小幅回落至周一的4.18%，显示市场在消化其表态后有所修正。 据CME FedWatch数据，交易员目前预计7月议息会议维持利率不变的概率高达85%，但9月加息25个基点的概率已升至52%。这意味着市场已将一次额外加息纳入基准情景，通胀扩散的持续性正在重塑美联储政策路径预期。 对投资者而言，当前局面的核心矛盾在于：通胀广度虽已超出历史常态，但尚未触发系统性风险；政策收紧预期升温，但节奏仍具不确定性。住房租金能否如期降温，将是下半年观察通胀走势的关键变量。 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。

德国 DDR5 内存价格飙至历史新高，装机成本大幅提升
articles.description: IT之家 7 月 20 日消息，DDR5 内存套装的价格仍在持续上涨，几乎每个月都能看到明显增长，如今已经达到历史最高水平。 今年 DDR5 内存价格已经涨到了令人难以置信的程度。即使 2026 年 1 月和 2 月的价格已经被认为是内存市场最糟糕的时期，7 月份的价格却进一步刷新历史纪录。 需要注意的是，这份数据可能无法完全代表全球 DDR5 内存价格趋势，但在对比不同地区当前 DDR5 内存套装价格时，仍具有较高参考价值。 根据 3D Center 的统计，德国市场目前多款 DDR5 内存套装的价格，仍接近 2025 年 7 月水平的 4 倍。 这份数据来自德国多家零售商，涵盖了多种 DDR5 内存规格，包括 8GB、16GB、32GB、24GB 和 48GB 容量版本。因此，能够较为准确地反映德国市场当前 DDR5 内存的价格状况。 虽然德国市场此前在今年 1 月和 2 月已经出现过最高价格，但 7 月份再次迎来大幅上涨，并打破了此前纪录。 DDR5 内存价格指数在 1 月和 2 月达到 440%，如今已经进一步升至惊人的 448%。 相比之下，6 月份的价格指数为 419%，涨幅非常明显。从相关数据表格来看，也可以清楚看到 DDR5 价格是如何一步步走到今天这一水平的。 此前，只有少数 DDR5 内存套装受到所谓“内存危机”的影响，但到了本月，几乎所有型号都出现了明显涨价。 IT之家注意到，唯一例外的是两款规格：2×48GB DDR5-6400 和 2×24GB DDR5-7200，这两种配置价格变化相对较小。 其中，2×16GB DDR5-6000 CL28 和 2×16GB DDR5-7200+ 成为了受影响最严重的型号，环比涨幅接近 16%～17%。 此外，还有多款 DDR5 内存套装出现突然上涨，涨幅在 2%～14% 之间。 总体来看，2026 年 7 月的 DDR5 内存价格已经达到去年以来最糟糕的水平，这让组装新电脑以及升级现有 PC 的成本越来越高，也让许多玩家的装机计划变得更加困难。

articles.description: IT之家 7 月 20 日消息，小米安全中心今日发布了一则 MiSRC 违规事件处置公告，称近期监测并核实到一起严重违规事件。 IT之家附公告如下： 事件概述 经安全团队应急响应调查核实： 2026 年 6 月 26 日下午时段，公司反入侵安全团队处置了一起影响范围广泛的入侵安全事件。 当晚，涉事白帽子刘 **（mid：278*****76）通过 MiSRC 平台提交了一份漏洞报告，报告内容与该入侵事件高度关联。其行为已构成实质性安全侵害，该白帽子的提交行为已严重超出正常漏洞挖掘范畴。 违规依据 该行为严重违反了 《小米安全中心安全漏洞奖励规则 V10.0》的基本原则： 小米反对和谴责以漏洞测试为借口，利用安全漏洞进行破坏、损害用户利益的黑客行为，包括但不仅限于利用漏洞盗取用户隐私及虚拟财产、入侵业务系统、非授权获取系统（业务）数据、窃取用户数据、恶意传播漏洞或数据等。如有上述行为，小米将有权追究其法律责任。 处理决定 经小米安全团队审议，作出如下处理决定： 漏洞奖励取消：涉事白帽子本次提交的漏洞取消所有奖励，相关漏洞不予计入任何荣誉或排名。 公开通报：对本次违规事件进行公开通报。 保留追究法律责任的权利：小米保留依据《中华人民共和国网络安全法》等相关法律法规，对涉事白帽子追究一切法律责任的权利。 郑重提醒 小米安全团队在此郑重提醒全体白帽子： 请严格遵守《小米安全中心安全漏洞奖励规则 V10.0》的各项要求； 安全测试必须在授权范围内进行，不得进行超出测试边界的渗透行为； 严禁利用 SRC 平台掩盖任何非法入侵或恶意行为； 任何试图以漏洞提交方式规避安全追溯的行为，小米安全团队将一追到底、严肃处理。 小米始终尊重并感谢每一位合规白帽子的技术贡献，但对任何违规行为将保持零容忍。让我们共同维护安全生态的底线，携手守护网络安全。 如有任何疑问，请通过 MiSRC 官方邮箱 security@xiaomi.com 反馈。 小米安全中心 2026 年 7 月

articles.title: 半导体指数跌入熊市，高盛悄然转向三大替代投资主题
articles.description: 半导体板块深陷熊市泥潭，令AI交易的吸引力大打折扣。高盛分析师团队随即推出三大替代投资主题，为寻求规避AI波动风险的投资者提供新的布局方向。 以英伟达、美光科技等AI芯片股为核心成分的费城半导体指数（SOX），已较约一个月前触及的盘中高点下跌逾20%，正式步入熊市区间。据MarketWatch报道，高盛分析师团队在上周五发布的研报中指出，AI基础设施股票的"痛苦波动"已促使投资者将目光转向AI主题以外的领域。 高盛由Ben Snider领衔的分析师团队由此提出三大替代方向：消费体验股、复利增长型企业（Compounders），以及并购潜在标的。这三类资产在估值、增长逻辑及风险特征上各有侧重，共同构成高盛在当前市场环境下的非AI投资框架。 消费体验股：抗AI扰动，估值具吸引力 高盛推荐的第一个主题是消费体验股。 高盛认为，这类股票"能够以合理估值获取消费者体验支出强劲长期增长的敞口，且受AI颠覆的风险有限"。 从数据来看，体验类消费支出增速已显著提速——涵盖运动中心、公园、剧院、博物馆及博彩等领域的体验消费增速，从2025年第一季度的1%（同期广义服务消费增速为2%）跃升至2026年第一季度的6%（同期广义服务消费增速仍为2%）。 高盛指出，这类消费在收入分布上偏向高端群体，且体验的实体属性使其相较于其他服务类别更能抵御AI的冲击。高盛在市值20亿美元以上的公司中筛选出36只候选标的。该主题的主要风险在于消费者健康状况恶化，包括油价上涨或劳动力市场走软。 复利增长型企业：质量溢价处于十年低位 第二个主题聚焦于高盛所称的"复利增长型企业"——即那些能够持续实现盈利增长、维持较高资本回报率并具备强劲自由现金流转化能力的公司。 高盛在罗素1000指数中，按历史及预期每股盈利增速、自由现金流转化率、投入资本回报率等多项成长与质量指标进行综合筛选，最终构建出包含15只个股的篮子，并明确剔除了"与AI最直接相关的股票，包括基础设施支出受益者及被认为面临颠覆风险的公司"。 估值方面，该篮子中位股的市盈率为22倍，高于标普500等权指数的16倍，但高盛测算，这一相对估值已接近十年低位。高盛认为，宏观环境与盈利增长前景均将对该类股票的估值形成支撑，但美联储转向鸽派或经济增长前景全面改善，将构成该主题的主要风险。 并购潜在标的：交易浪潮提供套利机会 第三个主题着眼于并购潜在标的。 高盛数据显示，今年并购活动大幅升温，已公告交易规模达1.2万亿美元，较2025年同期增长32%；已公告交易数量亦增加12%，其中40%集中于计算机与电子及医疗健康领域，但整体活动已扩散至多个行业。 高盛认为，宽松的金融条件、稳健的经济增长、较高的CEO信心以及友好的监管环境，共同构成并购活动持续推进的宏观支撑。该篮子包含71家公司，高盛分析师评估其被收购概率均超过15%。该主题的主要风险在于市场情绪转弱，进而威胁当前的并购周期。 AI交易降温，资金寻求再平衡 上述三大主题的推出，折射出当前市场的结构性变化。 费城半导体指数的熊市信号，标志着过去两年主导市场的AI叙事正面临阶段性考验，部分资金开始主动寻求分散配置。 从更广泛的市场表现来看，标普500指数年内仍上涨约8.94%，纳斯达克综合指数年内涨幅约9.80%，但过去一个月分别下跌0.57%和3.76%，显示科技板块承压明显。高盛此时推出非AI替代框架，时机上与市场情绪的微妙转变高度吻合，也为投资者在AI交易波动加剧背景下提供了一套可操作的再平衡思路。 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。

威刚陈立白：现阶段讨论 AI 泡沫言之过早，未来十年最短缺的资源是内存和电力
articles.description: IT之家 7 月 20 日消息，据台媒工商时报消息，威刚董事长陈立白表示，现阶段讨论 AI 泡沫言之过早，“2030 年以后，再来讨论 AI 泡沫究竟会在 2040 年还是 2050 年发生”，目前全球 AI 算力、内存及电力需求，仍远高于市场想象。 市场担忧云端服务商算力投资速度快于实际需求，甚至 Meta 开始对外出租部分运算资源。对此陈立白认为，不能因此推论 AI 需求不如预期。未来 AI 应用将全面扩展至企业对企业（B2B）、政府市场（B2G）、消费市场（B2C）及 B2B2C 等不同商业模式，算力需求规模将持续放大。 IT之家注意到，对于三星电子、SK 海力士及美光扩产，陈立白称三大原厂经历过去多次经济周期后，只会采取理性、审慎的扩产策略，不太可能重演无序大幅扩产。他认为，未来十年全球最短缺的两项资源，将是内存和电力（尤其是绿电）。 相关阅读： 《威刚预警：2026 年 Q3 内存将涨价 20%-30%，闪存将涨价 35%-40%》 《威刚 2026Q1 税后净利润同比增长 17 倍，单季超越去年总和》

articles.title: 研究：AI 会削弱人类批判性思维，降低人们说“我不知道”的意愿
articles.description: IT之家 7 月 20 日消息，2026 年，AI 依然会出现“幻觉”（hallucination），并且经常给出错误答案。 然而，法国和意大利多所大学的研究人员发现，获得 AI 建议后，人类的批判性思维能力可能会受到削弱，使人们更容易自信地复述 AI 提供的错误信息。 “对于人类来说，能够说‘我不知道’这一能力非常重要，因为这代表我们意识到了自身知识的局限。”米兰比可卡大学副教授 Valerio Capraro 在接受采访时表示，“但如今借助 AI，我们几乎可以轻松获得任何问题的答案。因此，我们想知道，这是否会影响人类承认‘我不知道’、暂缓判断的能力。” Capraro 与 École Normale Supérieure（法国高等师范学院）的 Chiara Marcoccia，以及罗马第一大学（Sapienza University of Rome）的 Walter Quattrociocchi 共同开展了一项研究，试图了解 AI 如何影响人们承认自己无知的意愿。 论文标题直接揭示了研究结论：《AI 建议会降低人们说“我不知道”的意愿，即使 AI 给出的建议是错误的且准确性是被鼓励的》。 AI 建议让人更少承认“不知道” Capraro 表示，他和团队设计了一组大型语言模型通常无法正确回答的问题。 据IT之家了解，在实验中，他们要求参与者回答一些关于电影视觉细节的问题，例如《我爱贝克汉姆》（Bend It Like Beckham）中球队球衣的颜色，或者电影《高速路上一只猫》（Like a Cat on a Highway）中 Monica 驾驶的车辆类型。 研究人员预计，这类细节通常不会出现在大多数 AI 模型的训练数据中，而实验所使用的模型（Step 3.5 Flash）也确实经常无法回答这些问题。 他们还测试了目前较新的前沿模型，包括 GPT-5.5、Claude Sonnet 4.6 和 Gemini 3.5 Flash。这些模型虽然在车辆问题上表现不佳，但经常能够正确回答其他细节问题。 研究人员选择 Step 3.5 Flash 的原因是，该模型在实验中通常会给出错误答案，这可以避免有人认为参与者只是合理地把判断权交给了一个可靠工具。 “我们将参与者分成两组。”Capraro 解释道，“一组需要在没有 AI 建议的情况下回答问题，另一组则可以向 AI 请求帮助。结果发现，在没有 AI 的情况下，有 44% 的人选择回答‘我不知道’，也就是暂缓判断。而在可以获得 AI 建议后，只有 3% 的人这么做。也就是说，人们暂停判断的能力几乎崩溃了。” AI 降低准确率，却提高自信程度 Capraro 表示，更令人意外的是，当 AI 提供帮助时，参与者的回答准确率也明显下降。换句话说，人们开始更加相信 AI 的答案，而不是自己的判断。 “在没有 AI 的情况下，有 27% 的人给出了正确答案。”他说，“但在获得 AI 建议后，只有 9% 的人回答正确。因此，一些原本可能答对的人，在询问 AI 后反而得到了错误答案。” 与此同时，AI 建议还显著提高了人们对自身答案的信心。Capraro 表示，在没有 AI 帮助时，参与者认为自己正确的比例约为 30%；而在使用 AI 后，这一比例上升到了 76%。 也就是说，即使 AI 存在幻觉问题，人们依然会相信它提供的信息。 “简单来说，人们的表现变得更差 —— 准确率只有原来的三分之一，但他们的自信程度却提高了一倍。”Capraro 说道。 金钱激励能改善情况，但效果有限 研究人员还进行了另一项实验，引入金钱奖励机制，希望鼓励参与者更加谨慎地判断。 结果显示，金钱激励确实带来了一定改善。选择暂缓判断、承认“不知道”的比例从 3% 提升到了 8%；回答正确的比例也从 9% 提升到了 16%。 不过，这两个数字仍然明显低于没有 AI 时的水平 —— 分别为 44% 和 27%。 虽然研究人员选择的是电影细节类问题，但他们认为，这一发现可以推广到其他领域。 Capraro 表示，他认为这一问题需要通过社会层面的 AI 素养教育和教育政策来解决。“当然，模型提供商也应该努力改善这一问题，但我认为双方的利益并不完全一致。”他说，“更有希望的解决方式，可能是在教育层面进行干预。” Capraro 特别担心 AI 对儿童成长带来的影响。 “成年人已经通过过去的学习经历培养了一定的批判性思维能力。”他说，“但对于那些从出生起就伴随着这些系统成长的孩子来说，风险在于，他们甚至可能无法真正学会最基本的批判性思考能力。”
